nameStory: The broad-faced sac spider gets its name from its notably wide, flat face compared to other sac spiders - imagine a spider that looks like it's been gently pressed from front to back! The 'sac' part of the name comes from their habit of building silken retreat sacs rather than traditional webs, like tiny sleeping bags tucked away in hidden spots.
description: The broad-faced sac spider is a medium-sized hunting spider that doesn't build webs to catch prey. Instead, it actively hunts at night and rests during the day in silken sacs it weaves in protected spots. These spiders have a distinctively flattened, broad face that sets them apart from their relatives, and they typically measure about half an inch in body length. Their bodies are usually pale yellow to light brown with darker markings.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctively broad, flattened face that looks wider than most spiders - feels almost turtle-like if you could touch it safely

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web for catching prey - instead builds small, silken retreat sacs that feel papery and are often found under bark or in crevices

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale yellow to light brown body with subtle darker markings that may appear slightly fuzzy or soft-textured

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized spider with body length around half an inch, about the size of a small button

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active nighttime hunter that moves deliberately and purposefully rather than scurrying quickly when disturbed

habitat: Found throughout New England's wooded areas, particularly under loose bark of dead or dying trees, in rock crevices, and around human structures like sheds and porches. They prefer slightly moist environments and are often discovered when splitting firewood or moving outdoor items that have been sitting still for a while.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots and beginning to hunt. Look for their silken sacs under bark and in protected crevices.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when hunting is most frequent and mating occurs. Most likely time to spot them moving at night near outdoor lights.
seasonality.fall: Females create egg sacs while adults prepare for winter by finding secure overwintering sites. Still active on warm autumn nights.
seasonality.winter: Adults hide in protected locations like deep bark crevices or inside buildings, becoming mostly inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being called 'sac spiders,' they don't live permanently in their silk retreats - they're more like spider hotels that get abandoned and rebuilt in new locations every few days as the spider roams its territory!
confusionNotes: Often confused with yellow sac spiders, but broad-faced sac spiders have that distinctively flattened, wide face that looks almost squished compared to the more typical spider head shape. Remember: if the face looks unusually broad and flat, you've likely found a broad-faced sac spider.
contextualKnowledge: The family name recently changed from Clubionidae to Trachelidae as scientists better understood spider relationships through genetic studies, so you might see this spider listed under different family names in older field guides.
compareHints: The broad-faced sac spider differs from its western relative, the bull-headed sac spider, primarily by geographic range - bull-headed sac spiders are found in western North America. Within New England, the distinctively flattened face shape is usually enough to distinguish it from other sac spider species, which tend to have more typically proportioned heads.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The bull-headed sac spider has a more dramatically enlarged and robust front section compared to its relative the broad-faced sac spider (Trachelas tranquillus).
